records.name: Liechtenstein
records.summary:
Liechtenstein is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Same-sex relations are legal and discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned, but gender identity, gender expression, and sex characteristics are not included in any anti-discrimination legislation, and there is no legal gender recognition law. These are resident-facing gaps: a visitor faces no legal exposure.

Liechtenstein is a very small, very low-crime Alpine country closely integrated with Switzerland; there is no documented pattern of anti-trans violence, no bathroom law, and no border friction (Schengen via Switzerland/Austria). Social attitudes are conservative but not mobilised-hostile. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): mixed situation - same-sex relations legal and sexual-orientation discrimination banned, but gender identity/expression/sex characteristics not covered by any anti-discrimination law; no legal gender marker change; IGM not prohibited; marriage and joint adoption available since January 2025; the state religion is Roman Catholicism and the archbishop publicly opposed marriage equality; first Pride in 2022.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature covers tiny European states (including Liechtenstein) playing catch-up on LGBT equality.
Euronews (May 2022): Austria to lower hurdles for LGBT citizens to donate blood - regional context relevant to Liechtenstein's customs-union neighbour (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Liechtenstein' (March 2012): with a population of ~35,000 there is no organised gay scene - friendship networks are the scene; 'few organized enemies... no religious extremists, no right-wing skinheads, no political rogues demanding homophobic laws'; gay people live comfortably with little interference.

360° magazine (Jan 2016, in French): Prince Hans-Adam II called rainbow families 'irresponsible' in his New Year interview, said children have 'a right to a normal family', and suggested Liechtenstein could 'ignore' an adverse European Court of Human Rights ruling; local LGBT organisation Flay said it was 'choqué'; the Freie Liste called the remarks contrary to the Constitution and the ECHR.

Landtag motion (Sept 2022, in German): 'Motion zur Öffnung der Ehe für alle' - MPs' motion to open civil marriage regardless of gender and sexual orientation, removing all remaining legal differences; notes registered partnerships are seen as a 'second-class marriage' and that the Prince had said in 2021 he had nothing against marriage equality except adoption.

records.name: Sri Lanka
records.summary:
Sri Lanka is dangerous for trans visitors. Sections 365/365A of the 1883 Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and Human Dignity Trust lists Sri Lanka as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and “cheating by personation” provisions against trans people. The International Commission of Jurists identifies Sri Lanka Police as “the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals” — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. Colombo has a small organised community (EQUAL GROUND) and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Sections 365/365A of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women); prosecutions limited but harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services are frequent; no comprehensive anti-discrimination protections; authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence - widely condemned as torture. Legal gender recognition is possible (via a certification process).
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Sri Lanka's criminalisation of same-sex activity.

ICJ opinion piece (Aug 2023) by Mathuri Thamilmaran: 'Protecting transgender persons: Going beyond rule by circular' - the Sri Lanka Police are the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals; recent months saw both the Police and the Human Rights Commission acknowledging this; argues administrative circulars are insufficient without legal reform.

UK Home Office CPIN Sri Lanka: Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (v6.0, Sept 2024): assessment of risk from state and non-state actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information.

US State Department country report for Sri Lanka (custom URL): official human-rights assessment including the SOGI section - criminalisation under the penal code and police harassment of LGBT persons.

Joint UPR stakeholder report (EQUAL GROUND, Northwestern CIHR, GIHR) for Sri Lanka's 3rd cycle: 'Human Rights Violations Against LGBTIQ Individuals in Sri Lanka' - documents criminalisation and violations by the coalition of NGOs for UPR.

Canada IRB Response to Information Request LKA103948.E (Jan 2012): 'Treatment of sexual minorities in Sri Lanka' - Article 365 criminalises 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' (up to 10 years, men only); Article 365A 'gross indecency' (both sexes, amended 1995 to cover women); rarely enforced with no convictions, but criminalisation 'paves the way for police and anti-gay groups to brand all lesbian, bisexual, transgendered persons as perverts and criminals'.

records.name: Lesotho
records.summary: Lesotho demands real caution. Same-sex conduct is legal (sodomy common-law crime struck down in 2012); the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho documents failures to prevent violence, harassment and discrimination by state and non-state actors (2024 UPR submission); no LGR; small organised community inside South Africa's geographic envelope.

sources.claim: Joint stakeholder UPR report (Oct 2024) by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho on LGBTQ+ rights in Lesotho: documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and community-level SOGIESC discrimination; same-sex conduct is not criminalised but no protections exist.

ICJ UPR submission (Nov 2024) on Lesotho: highlights LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination among three key concerns (alongside inclusive education for children with disabilities and revocation of NGO lawyers' practising certificates).

SALC + People's Matrix Association + WLSA briefing (Oct 2020): 'Legal Gender Recognition in Lesotho' - analysis of law and policy against international best practice; Matrix is the only known LGBTI organisation in Lesotho; researched by Prof Alex Müller with community consultations.

US State Department 2016 Human Rights Report for Lesotho: documents the LDF mutiny arrests, torture of detainees, the killing of Lt-Gen Mahao, and the LGBT section noting no criminalisation but societal stigma.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Lesotho' (2017): constitutional analysis - section 4(1) 'sex' and 'other status' should include gender identity per the UN Human Rights Committee; no law allows gender-marker changes; a trans person using a non-matching passport could be charged; the Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omits gender and sexual orientation.

Lesotho Labour Act 2024 (full text, ILO NATLEX): the new labour law - unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, forced and child labour prohibitions - the current statutory framework for workplace rights.

records.name: Lithuania
records.summary:
Lithuania is broadly workable, at the lower end, with one of Europe's most restrictive legal-gender-recognition situations. The Civil Code grants the right to medically change gender in principle, but there has been no legal framework regulating the procedure for 17 years — a deadlock the Constitutional Court refused to resolve in September 2025, perpetuating what an ECtHR body called a "distressing legal uncertainty."

Socially, a conservative climate is well documented: an MP called LGBT people "degenerated" and "spreading diseases" (his immunity was revoked), "traditional family values" groups disrupt peaceful protests, the Seimas Ombudsperson found police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to assembly, and trans people report systemic workplace harassment — open ridicule, isolation, and psychological abuse. A "Protection of Minors" law limits dissemination of LGBT information (a 2024 Constitutional Court ruling weakened its same-sex-family provision). There is no criminalisation, and LT Pride 2024 drew 15,000.

sources.claim: LGL (Lithuanian Gay League) news (Sept 2025): the Constitutional Court refused to address Lithuania's 18-year trans rights gap - a significant setback; the Civil Code grants unmarried adults the right to medically change gender but implementing legislation has never been adopted, leaving trans people in legal limbo.

LGL news (Aug 2025): could courts finally end 17 years of legal limbo for transgender rights? - the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court suspended a civil case on amending civil-status gender documents and referred the question of the laws' compliance with the Constitution to the Constitutional Court.

LRT (Sept 2025): Lithuania's Constitutional Court declined to examine a lower court's request to review the absence of legal provisions allowing trans people to change gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents.
LRT (May 2025): trans people in Lithuania detail workplace harassment - open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse; systemic labour-market discrimination per experts.

LGL news (April 2024): the Seimas Ombudsperson found that police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly - inadequate police response to hostile provocateurs at an LGL assembly; recommended measures to guarantee effective assembly rights.

Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson, 'The Situation of Transgender People in Lithuania - Summary of the National Review 2024': second national review (after 2019) covering public attitudes, the legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and negative public attitudes; notes the lack of a legal framework and strategic approach.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Lithuania: systemic lack of targeted LGBTI hate-crime victim support; LGBTI asylum seekers from Cameroon granted protection after a four-year wait, with dire camp conditions and a psychologist convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts; prosecution of former MP Gražulis for anti-LGBTI ridicule complicated by his MEP immunity.

PinkNews (Sept 2013): Lithuania's parliament to consider five anti-gay and anti-trans bills - a ban on gender reassignment ('gender is determined genetically from the very moment of conception'), a same-sex adoption ban, fines up to €1,800 for organisers of events 'denigrating constitutional moral values', and legalisation of anti-gay speech.

PinkNews (July 2009): Lithuania's parliament passed a 'Section 28-style' law banning information on homosexuality in schools and media accessible to minors ('Law on the Protection of Minors'), overriding President Adamkus's veto 87-6; Amnesty called it 'a huge step backwards'.

records.name: Luxembourg
records.summary:
Luxembourg is exceptionally safe — one of Europe's strongest trans jurisdictions. Legal gender recognition by self-determination since 2018 (Act of 10 August 2018), with no medical requirements, and notably the process is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned across employment, goods, services, education, and health; a national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018; an equality body (CET) handles complaints.

No traveler-facing concerns exist: no bathroom laws, no border issues (Schengen), no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Gaps are minor: no nonbinary marker, and gender expression/sex characteristics are not explicitly covered in anti-discrimination law.

sources.claim: Official Luxembourg government portal (Guichet.lu) page on applying to change one's gender status and first name(s) in the civil register - the administrative procedure for legal gender recognition.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): marriage and adoption; self-determination-based gender markers (no nonbinary markers); discrimination banned on sexual orientation and gender identity but not gender expression or sex characteristics; no measures on conversion practices or intersex interventions; in July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan, criticised by organisations for missing depathologisation and other key elements.

Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale UPR submission (April 2023) for Luxembourg: describes the organisation's services and Luxembourg's equality laws (employment, goods and services, education, health), the CET equality body and the national LGBTI action plan.

Asher Fergusson's LGBTQ+ Travel Safety Index (updated June 2023): 400+ hours of research ranking all countries' laws for LGBTQ+ traveller safety, with a companion Global Transgender Rights Index - comparative data source covering Luxembourg.

Le Quotidien (June 2019, in French): 'Agressions LGBTphobes: un durcissement des sanctions attendu' - Luxembourg law lacks LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances; victims under-report; the justice minister signalled the law would evolve after ECRI's 2017 intervention.

Le Quotidien (May 2017, in French): Justice Minister Félix Braz presented a bill allowing trans and intersex people to change civil-status gender by declaration - replacing the long, costly judicial procedure; welcomed by associations.

Le Quotidien (July 2018, in French): the Chamber approved bill 7146 simplifying gender and first-name changes for trans people (57-3, only ADR opposed) - change by written request with supporting documents, no medical requirements.

records.name: Latvia
records.summary:
Latvia is broadly workable with no legal framework for gender recognition — trans people cannot legally change their gender marker, leaving those who've transitioned in a legal limbo. The most documented institutional failure is the European Court of Human Rights ruling Hanovs v. Latvia (2024), which found Latvia failed to prosecute a homophobic hate crime (the 2021 attack on lecturer Deniss Hanovs), violating the prohibition of inhuman treatment and the right to private life. There is no criminalisation, and bathrooms are unrestricted.

On the positive side, an administrative court overturned the denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI asylum-seeker in 2025, showing some institutional capacity for protection. The documented hostility is less extreme than in Lithuania (no "degenerate"-rhetoric MP, no propaganda-style minors law, no systemic-trans-workplace-harassment study surfaced), which places Latvia marginally above its southern neighbour.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying LSM article (June 2025) covers transgender and non-binary Latvians facing a struggle for recognition.

ECtHR press release, Hanovs v. Latvia (18 July 2024): the Court unanimously found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 after a 2020 homophobic attack - no criminal charges were brought despite the aggressor admitting anti-gay slurs; the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter with a lenient fine, fostering impunity for hate-motivated offences.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Latvia: an administrative court overturned denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI seeker; the Prosecutor General reopened criminal proceedings in the Khanov hate-crime case after the ECtHR ruling; two people attacked in Daugavpils, with the Prosecutor General ordering the investigation reopened after police closed it; former MEP Mamikins' homophobic posts investigated (he fled to Russia).

Strasbourg Observers analysis (Nov 2024) of Hanovs v. Latvia: further clarification of states' positive obligations in homophobic-attack cases - states must thoroughly investigate and punish hate crimes, sending a message of zero tolerance; notes the troubling pattern of Eastern European states failing to protect LGBTI+ persons and to investigate effectively.

ILGA-Europe Latvia page: includes the July 2024 ECtHR judgment in Hanovs v. Latvia - the Court found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 after Latvian authorities declined to prosecute a homophobic assault on a gay couple in Riga as a hate-motivated offence.

PinkNews (May 2007): Archbishop of Riga Cardinal Janis Pujats called homosexuality 'total corruption in the sexual arena' and 'an unnatural form of prostitution', demanded a referendum on same-sex marriage and crowds of 40,000-50,000 to counter Pride, calling Pride a 'foreign-inspired action'.
Xinhua (June 2018): around 8,000 people marched in Baltic Pride 2018 in Riga - the annual event rotated among Baltic capitals; organised by Mozaika under the motto 'See Diversity! See Freedom!'.

records.name: Macau
records.summary:
A small southern Chinese territory with its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation: nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression, and almost nothing protects them either. There is no legal gender-recognition pathway — the first organised push (2015) got only a hearing at the identification bureau, with the trans claimant speaking behind a screen; when government legislated on domestic violence in 2016 it knowingly excluded same-sex partners as non-'family', against a 2015 UN Committee-Against-Torture direction that protection be non-discriminatory — an exclusion a local association and an internationally known campaigner publicly accused the administration of choosing, warning it signals SOGI bias is justifiable.

For a visitor: zero legal risk, near-zero legal recourse, and the compression of a very small city where casinos, churches and old resident networks all know their own. The administration treats the subject as a non-issue — which is both the mercy and the void.

sources.claim: Macau Daily Times (Feb 2015): Rainbow of Macau met Identification Bureau officials to discuss changing gender on Macau ID documents - one individual ('Avery', speaking behind a screen) sought the change; the first organised push for gender recognition in Macau.

Macau Daily Times (May 2016): Rainbow of Macau criticised the government for excluding same-sex relationships from domestic-violence legislation because same-sex partners were not considered 'family members'.

Jason Chao / Rainbow of Macau statement (May 2016): the government knowingly enacted a discriminatory domestic-violence law despite the UN Committee against Torture's 2015 concluding observations requiring protection without discrimination; warns the law signals that sexual-orientation discrimination is justifiable.

records.name: Morocco
records.summary:
Morocco is dangerous for trans visitors. Article 489 criminalises same-sex “indecent acts” (6 months–3 years), and Cairo 52 documents that trans people face de-facto criminalisation under Article 498 morality provisions — arrests based on gender-expression discrepancies and forced outing. The 2026 Cairo 52 report “A Web of Violence” describes a legal-medical-social system of erasure for trans people, including a de facto prohibition on transition care.

Visitor-relevant cases exist: in 2024, Brazilian influencer Liziane Gutierrez was arrested in Marrakesh, accused by police of being transgender, and alleges she was forced to show her genitals — she spent a month in jail. In 2019, Marrakesh police filmed and humiliated a cross-dressing man after a traffic accident, leaking the video online. There is no LGR framework and police have wide discretion; tourist areas (Marrakesh, Agadir) are more tolerant in practice but the legal exposure is constant.

The Gutierrez case demonstrates that even a cisgender visitor suspected of being trans can face genital inspection and jail.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 report 'A Web of Violence: The Systemic Erasure of Transgender People in Morocco' (Jan 2026, by Hamzawya and Nora Noralla): based on interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans - documents an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility; Morocco once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreigners but now enforces a de facto prohibition for its own citizens; Article 489 weaponised to arrest trans people based on gender expression; no legal gender recognition pathway.

Cairo 52 country review of Morocco: no specific provisions on transition, but de facto criminalisation under Article 498 (moral charges, gender-expression discrepancies, involuntary outing); no gender-affirming healthcare framework, leading some to self-medicate; a 2021 recognition process exists for intersex people only; the Grand Mufti opposes transition.
Hindustan Times (Nov 2024): an Instagram model alleges Moroccan police forced her to show her genitals over trans suspicions - reported police abuse of a trans woman based on appearance.

El País (Jan 2019): Moroccan police subjected a Marrakesh cross-dresser to online humiliation - after a minor traffic accident, Chafiq was handcuffed and filmed by bystanders and police officers, who also photographed his ID documents and posted them online; he sought asylum in Europe. Homosexuality is punishable in Morocco.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Article 489 criminalises 'indecent acts' between persons of the same sex (6 months to 3 years) with wide police discretion and arbitrary arrests; 170 people charged with same-sex relations in 2018; HRW documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment of presumed gay and bisexual men; no legal gender recognition; public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence and harassment; authorities block LGBTIQ organisations.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - includes Morocco's Article 489 criminalisation and the annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA.
ILGA 'State-Sponsored Homophobia' (May 2008, Daniel Ottosson): world survey of laws prohibiting same-sex activity between consenting adults - country-by-country legal survey including Morocco.
Washington Blade (Sept 2014): the UN Human Rights Council adopted the SOGI resolution - international context for human-rights scrutiny of countries including Morocco.
